english_translation: A wide tarred road shows cars passing each other in opposite directions. Along the edge of this road stand large, mature trees. Beneath these trees lies dry grass that looks as though it has not been rained on for a long time.

dialogue.shona: Mugwagwa wakapamhamha une tara unoratidza kuti une motokari dzirikupesana.
dialogue.english: A wide tarred road shows cars passing one another.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('wakapamhamha')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'wakapamhamha' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('unoratidza')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'unoratidza' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('Pasi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'Pasi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

cultural_notes.title: Getting Around: Kombis, Buses, Rural Carts & 'Robots'
cultural_notes.content: Daily transport in Zimbabwe features unique local vocabulary! In towns and cities, most commuters travel by white commuter minibuses universally called 'makombi' (singular: 'kombi'), while long-distance intercity trips use large buses ('bhazi') and heavy haulage trucks are affectionately nicknamed 'magonyeti'. In rural areas, donkey-drawn carts ('ngoro yemadhongi') are widely used to carry goods. And if someone tells you to turn at the 'robhoti' (plural: 'marobhotsi'), they don't mean a machine person—in Zimbabwe and Southern Africa, traffic lights are called 'robots'!

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Vanhu vakamira pamusika vachimirira kukwira bhazi.'
options: The driver stopped the car near the traffic lights.
People are standing at the market waiting to board the bus.
We saw two large trucks carrying maize to the city.
The road to the eastern highlands has many curves.
active_exercises.correct_answer: People are standing at the market waiting to board the bus.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Vanhu vakamira pamusika' = 'People are standing at the market', 'vachimirira kukwira bhazi' = 'waiting to board the bus'.

active_exercises.prompt: In a Zimbabwean city, if a driver says 'Mota dzakamira parobhoti dzichimirira mwenje wegirinhi', where are the cars stopped?
options: At a rural bus stop waiting for passengers
Inside a garage having their tyres repaired
At the traffic light waiting for the green light
Beside a river bridge that is under construction
active_exercises.correct_answer: At the traffic light waiting for the green light
active_exercises.explanation: 'Robhoti' (plural 'marobhotsi') is the standard Shona word for a traffic light, and 'mwenje wegirinhi' is the green light.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new family sentence into English: 'Hanzvadzi yangu inoshanda muguta reHarare.'
options: My parents live at the rural homestead in Masvingo.
My friend passed all her school examinations this year.
The baby is sleeping quietly inside the bedroom.
My sibling works in the city of Harare.
active_exercises.correct_answer: My sibling works in the city of Harare.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Hanzvadzi yangu' = 'My sibling (brother/sister)', 'inoshanda' = 'works', 'muguta reHarare' = 'in the city of Harare'.
